q: State the output of this program. (2)
code:
for i in range(3):
    print(i)
ms: Output: 0, 1, 2 on separate lines. Why: range(3) starts at 0 and produces exactly 3 values, stopping BEFORE 3. Remember: range(n) = n values starting from zero — if you wrote 1 2 3, you've hit the most common range trap.

q: State the output of this program. (2)
code:
for i in range(1, 4):
    print(i * 10)
ms: Output: 10, 20, 30. Why: range(1, 4) gives 1, 2, 3 (stop is exclusive — one before 4), and each is multiplied by 10. Remember: 'stops one early' — to reach 4 you would need range(1, 5).

q: State the output of this program. (2)
code:
for i in range(10, 0, -2):
    print(i)
ms: Output: 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. Why: start 10, step -2, stop before 0 — so 0 itself is never printed. Remember: countdowns need the negative step; the stop value is excluded in both directions.

q: State the output when the user enters **85**. (3)
ms: Output: Merit — one line only. Why: 85 fails the first test (85 < 90), passes the second (85 >= 70), and once a branch runs the WHOLE chain is finished — the mark >= 50 test is never even looked at. Remember: elif chains fire exactly one branch, the first True one.

q: State the output when `n = 20`. (3)
ms: Output: Big AND Very big (two lines). Why: these are three SEPARATE ifs, not an elif chain — each is tested independently. 20 > 10 True, 20 > 15 True, 20 > 25 False. Remember the contrast: separate ifs can all fire; an elif chain fires exactly one. Exams switch between the two to catch skim-readers.

q: State the output. (3)
code:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 6):
    total = total + i
print(total)
ms: Output: 15. Why: range(1, 6) gives 1,2,3,4,5, and total grows 0→1→3→6→10→15. One print AFTER the loop shows only the final value. Method to trust: trace the total column value by value — never sum in your head, the range endpoints are where errors hide.

q: State the output. (3)
code:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 6):
    total = total + i
    print(total)
ms: Output: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 — five lines. Why: identical maths to the previous style of question, but print is INDENTED inside the loop, so the running total shows after every addition. Remember: indentation decides 'every pass' vs 'once at the end' — check where the print sits before answering.

q: State the output. (3)
ms: Output: 1, 2, 3, 4. Why: when i reaches 5, break kills the loop IMMEDIATELY — before the print, because the if comes first in the body. So 5 is never printed and neither is anything after. Remember: break = leave the loop now; nothing else in this pass or any later pass runs.

q: State the output. (3)
ms: Output: 1, 2, 4, 5 — only 3 is missing. Why: continue abandons just that one pass (skipping the print for i = 3) and the loop carries on with 4. Contrast with break, which would have stopped everything at 3. Memory hook: break kills the loop, continue skips the lap.

q: State the output, showing your working. (3)
code:
x = 1
while x < 50:
    x = x * 2
print(x)
ms: Output: 64. Working: x doubles 1→2→4→8→16→32→64. The subtle step: when x = 32 the test 32 < 50 is still True, so it doubles ONE more time to 64; only then does 64 < 50 fail. Remember: the loop body runs for every value that PASSES the test — trace one step past where you think it stops.

q: State the output. (3)
code:
n = 7
while n > 7:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
print("Done")
ms: Output: Done — nothing else. Why: while checks BEFORE the first pass, and 7 > 7 is False immediately, so the body runs zero times. The unindented print("Done") is outside the loop and always runs. Remember: a while loop can legitimately run zero times — that's what 'pre-condition loop' means.

q: State the output. (3)
ms: Output, six lines: 0 0 / 0 1 / 0 2 / 1 0 / 1 1 / 1 2. Why: the inner loop finishes COMPLETELY (j = 0,1,2) for each outer value, so the left number sticks while the right one spins. Count check: 2 × 3 = 6 lines. Method: trace nested loops in a grid — outer fixed, inner cycling.

q: State the output. (3)
code:
for i in range(1, 4):
    print("*" * i)
ms: Output: * then ** then *** (a growing triangle). Why: * with a string means REPEAT, and the repeat count is the loop variable, so each line gains a star. Remember: string * number = repetition; this triangle pattern is a favourite for testing exactly that.

q: State the output. (4)
ms: Output: 4. Why: range(20) is 0..19, and i % 5 == 0 is True for the multiples of 5 in that range: 0, 5, 10, 15 — note 0 counts (0 % 5 = 0) and 20 is excluded by range. So four hits. Two traps in one question: forgetting 0 is a multiple, and letting 20 sneak in. Trace the multiples explicitly before counting.

q: State the output when the user enters **y** then **n**. (3)
code:
count = 0
again = "y"
while again == "y":
    count = count + 1
    again = input()
print(count)
ms: Output: 2. Trace it: the flag starts "y" so pass 1 runs (count = 1) and reads "y" → still "y", pass 2 runs (count = 2) and reads "n" → test fails, loop ends, prints 2. Why tracing matters: the loop keeps going one pass per "y" PLUS the initial flag pass — guessing usually lands one off. Rule: with while loops and inputs, trace pass-by-pass, marking what each input() consumes.

q: State the output. (3)
ms: Output: B only. Working each condition: and needs BOTH — x > 2 True but y > 10 False → no A. or needs ONE — x > 2 True → B prints. not flips — x == 3 is True, so not True = False → no C. Method: evaluate each comparison to True/False first, then apply and/or/not. Never judge compound conditions by feel.

q: State the output when the user enters **15**. (3)
ms: Output: Odd. Why: 15 % 2 = 1, so the outer condition fails and Python jumps straight to else — the inner 'Big even' test is NESTED inside the True branch and is never reached, even though 15 > 10. Remember: a nested if only exists for values that got past the outer one.

q: State the output. (3)
code:
result = 0
i = 10
while i >= 2:
    result = result + 1
    i = i // 2
print(result, i)
ms: Output: 3 1. Trace: i goes 10 → 5 → 2 → 1, and the body runs for each value that passes the >= 2 test: 10 ✓, 5 ✓, 2 ✓, then 1 ✗. So result counts 3 passes, and i finishes at 1. Both values print on ONE line (comma in print = same line, space between). Remember: // floors, and count the passes, not the arrows.

q: State the output when the user enters **0**. (3)
code:
n = int(input())
while n != 0:
    print("Processing", n)
    n = int(input())
print("Finished")
ms: Output: Finished — nothing else. Why: the sentinel 0 was entered FIRST, and while tests before running, so the body is skipped entirely (zero passes) and only the line after the loop runs. This is the pre-condition loop's defining behaviour, and exactly why sentinel loops read one value BEFORE the loop — so the sentinel itself is never processed.

q: State the output. (4)
code:
biggest = 0
nums = [4, 9, 2, 7]
for n in nums:
    if n > biggest:
        biggest = n
        print("New:", biggest)
print("Final:", biggest)
ms: Output: New: 4 / New: 9 / Final: 9. Trace: 4 > 0 → biggest 4, message. 9 > 4 → biggest 9, message. 2 > 9? No — silent. 7 > 9? No — silent. Then the final line. Why 2 and 7 print nothing: the print is INSIDE the if, so only improvements speak. Remember: check which prints are guarded by the if and which aren't before predicting output.

q: State the output. (3)
ms: Output: 1 0 / 2 0 / 2 1 — three lines. The twist: the INNER range depends on i. i = 0 → range(0) = zero passes (nothing); i = 1 → j = 0 only; i = 2 → j = 0, 1. Total passes 0+1+2 = 3. Remember: when the inner range uses the outer variable, work each outer value separately — the triangle pattern 0+1+2+… is the give-away.

q: State the output. (3)
ms: Output: e, x. Why: for c in word walks the characters e, x, a, m in order; at 'a' the break fires BEFORE the print, ending the loop — so neither 'a' nor 'm' appears. Two facts tested at once: strings are looped character-by-character, and break exits before finishing the pass.

q: State the output when the user enters **25** then **8** then **50**. (3)
ms: Output: 22. Trace each input: 25 → >= 20 → +10 (total 10); 8 → else → +2 (total 12); 50 → +10 (total 22). Why the method matters: loop-plus-if questions want you to run the decision fresh for EVERY input — the mark scheme follows the same three rows your trace table should have.

q: State the output. (3)
code:
a = True
b = False
print(a and b)
print(a or b)
print(not a)
ms: Output: False / True / False. Straight from the truth tables: and needs both (True and False = False); or needs one (True or False = True); not flips (not True = False). These three lines ARE the truth-table facts — if any felt uncertain, rewrite the three rules until they're reflex.

q: State the output, and explain why the loop ends when it does. (4)
code:
pw = "cat"
guess = ""
tries = 0
while guess != pw and tries < 3:
    guess = input()
    tries = tries + 1
print(tries)

The user enters: dog, cow, cat
ms: Output: 3. Trace: pass 1 reads dog (tries 1), pass 2 cow (tries 2), pass 3 cat (tries 3). The next test then fails because guess == pw — the FIRST half of the and is now False, and and needs both sides True to continue. Note the loop would also have stopped at tries = 3 even for a wrong third guess — two exit routes, either one ends it. Compound while-conditions: check both halves at every test.

q: State the output. (3)
ms: Output: A, B. The subtlety: the else belongs ONLY to the second if (the one directly above it). n > 0 → A prints. n > 2 → B prints, so its else (C) is skipped. If n had been 1: A would print, then C — because the second if fails. Remember: an else pairs with the nearest if at the same indentation, not with all the ifs above.

q: State the output. (3)
code:
msg = ""
for i in range(4):
    msg = msg + str(i)
print(msg)
ms: Output: 0123 — one string, one line. Why: str(i) converts each number to text and + JOINS strings, so msg grows "0" → "01" → "012" → "0123". Not 6 (that would be adding numbers) and not four separate lines (the print is outside the loop). Type awareness first, then trace.

q: State the output when the user enters **3**. (4)
ms: Output, three lines: '1 2 3' / '2 4 6' / '3 6 9' — a 3×3 multiplication square. Why: the outer loop picks the row number i; the inner builds one whole row (i×1, i×2, i×3) into the string 'line', which is printed ONCE per row because print sits in the outer body. Also note line = "" resets INSIDE the outer loop — that's what stops rows accumulating. Structure-reading like this is what nested-loop questions really test.

q: State the output. (3)
code:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 8, 2):
    total = total + i
print(total)
ms: Output: 16. First list the range values — start 1, step 2, stop before 8: 1, 3, 5, 7. Then sum: 16. The trap: including 8 would need range(1, 9, 2) — students who 'read' the 8 as included get 24 and lose the marks. ALWAYS write out a stepped range's values before doing anything with them.

q: State the output when the user enters **6** then **6**. (3)
ms: Output: Equal. Why: with 6 and 6 both comparisons are False (6 > 6 fails both ways), so the else — the 'neither' catcher — runs. This is the standard three-way comparison shape: greater / less / else-must-be-equal. Remember that else needs no condition precisely because it means 'everything left over'.

q: This loop should print 1 to 10 but prints 1 to 9. Identify the fault, name the error type, and correct the line. (3)
ms: Fault: range(1, 10) stops BEFORE 10 — the stop value is always excluded (1). Error type: logic error — it runs fine but under-counts (1). Correction: for i in range(1, 11): (1). Fix the habit, not just the line: whenever a loop must INCLUDE n, the range's stop is n + 1.
code:
for i in range(1, 10):
    print(i)

q: This program never stops. Identify the fault, name the error type, and state the fix. (3)
ms: Fault: the body never changes n, so n > 0 stays True forever (1). Error type: logic error — an infinite loop (1). Fix: add n = n - 1 inside the loop body (1). The diagnostic rule: 'never stops' = go straight to the while condition and ask WHICH variable it tests, then check whether the body ever updates that variable.

q: This program should greet choices "A" or "B" only, but greets everything. Identify the fault, name the error type, and correct the condition. (3)
ms: Fault: the right-hand side of or is the bare string "B", not a comparison — Python treats any non-empty string as True, so the whole condition is always True (1). Error type: logic error (1). Correction: if choice == "A" or choice == "B": (1). Burn this in: EACH side of and/or must be a complete comparison — 'x == 1 or 2' is the most-planted trap in the paper.

q: This validation loop never exits, whatever is typed. Identify the fault, name the error type, and correct the condition. (3)
ms: Fault: with or, any answer differs from at least ONE of "Y"/"N", so the condition is always True (type "Y": it's still != "N") (1). Error type: logic error (1). Correction: while ans != "Y" and ans != "N": (1). Rule to remember: staying-in-a-loop over several forbidden values needs AND ('it isn't this AND isn't that'); or makes the loop immortal.

q: A £60 basket is charged £2.99 delivery instead of free. Identify the fault, name the error type, and correct the code. (3)
ms: Fault: the chain tests total > 20 FIRST, and £60 passes it — so the free-delivery branch can never be reached by anyone (1). Error type: logic error from wrongly ordered conditions (1). Correction: test the most generous band first — if total > 50: free, elif total > 20: 2.99, else: 4.99 (1). Whenever tiered pricing/grading misfires, check the ORDER of the elif chain before anything else.

q: This program should print "Teen" for ages 13 to 19 inclusive, but 13 and 19 print nothing. Identify the fault, name the error type, and correct the line. (3)
ms: Fault: > and < EXCLUDE the boundaries — 13 > 13 is False (1). Error type: logic (boundary) error (1). Correction: if age >= 13 and age <= 19: (1). Boundary checking discipline: test your condition mentally with the two edge values themselves; 'inclusive' in the question always means >= and <=.

q: This countdown prints nothing. Identify the fault, name the error type, and correct the line. (3)
ms: Fault: range(5, 0) tries to count UP from 5 to 0 with the default step +1, which is impossible, so the range is empty (1). Error type: logic error (1). Correction: for i in range(5, 0, -1): (1). Remember: counting down ALWAYS needs an explicit negative step — Python never infers direction.
code:
for i in range(5, 0):
    print(i)

q: This program should stop reading when "END" is typed, but processes "END" as a real answer first. Identify the fault and rewrite the loop correctly. (3)
ms: Fault: the input is read and processed INSIDE the loop before any check, so "END" gets counted before the test can stop the loop (1). Fix — the sentinel pattern: read the first answer BEFORE the loop, test in the while condition, and read the next answer at the END of the body (2). Pattern: prime the pump before the loop; refill at the bottom. That ordering is exactly what keeps the sentinel out of the data.
code:
count = 0
while True:
    ans = input()
    count = count + 1
    if ans == "END":
        break
print(count)

q: The bonus should need a key AND (a torch OR a rope), but a player with only a rope gets it. Identify the fault, name the error type, and correct the condition. (3)
ms: Fault: without brackets, and binds tighter than or, so this reads (key and torch) or rope — a bare rope satisfies the right side alone (1). Error type: logic error (1). Correction: if key and (torch or rope): (1). Rule: whenever and and or share a condition, BRACKET the or — precedence will not read your mind.
code:
if key and torch or rope:
    print("Bonus")

q: This loop should total five entered numbers but outputs only the last one. Identify the fault, name the error type, and show the corrected structure. (3)
ms: Fault: total = 0 sits INSIDE the loop, so the pot is emptied at the start of every pass — only the final number survives (1). Error type: logic error (1). Correction: move total = 0 ABOVE the for line (1). Memory hook: zero the pot BEFORE collecting. Symptom→cause pairing worth memorising: 'output equals just the last input' = initialisation inside the loop.
code:
for i in range(5):
    total = 0
    n = int(input())
    total = total + n
print(total)

q: State the output, then state what single change would make it print 5 lines of "Hello". (3)
ms: Output as written: one "Hello" — the print is NOT indented, so the loop body is empty-ish (in fact this exact code raises an IndentationError in strict Python because the for has no body; treat it as printing once if your editor auto-fixes). The exam point (2 marks): indent print("Hello") under the for and it becomes the loop body, running 5 times (1). Indentation isn't decoration in Python — it decides what the loop owns.
code:
for i in range(5):
print("Hello")

q: Trace this program for entered values **4, 0, 7, -1** and state every line of output. (4)
ms: Output: Even (for 4) / Zero (for 0) / Odd (for 7) / Bye. Walk it: 4 → not zero, 4 % 2 == 0 → Even. 0 → FIRST branch catches it (Zero) — order matters, since 0 % 2 == 0 would also be True, but the chain stops at the first hit. 7 → Odd. -1 → the while test fails, loop ends, Bye. Two lessons: sentinel -1 is never classified, and the Zero test must come before the Even test precisely because elif takes the first match.

q: State how many times "tick" is printed, and how you calculated it. (3)
ms: "tick" prints 20 times. Calculation: the inner loop's 5 passes happen in FULL for each of the outer's 4 passes — 4 × 5 = 20 (and "round" prints 4 times, once per outer pass). The rule doing the work: the inner loop completes entirely for every single outer iteration, so nested totals are always outer × inner.

q: State the output. (3)
code:
n = 0
while n < 3:
    n = n + 1
    print(n)
print(n)
ms: Output: 1, 2, 3, then 3 again. Why: the increment comes BEFORE the print inside the loop, so passes show 1, 2, 3; the loop exits when n = 3 fails the test n < 3, and the final unindented print repeats the surviving value 3. Watch for: order of lines WITHIN the body changes what's shown (increment-then-print vs print-then-increment), and variables keep their final value after a loop.

q: State the output when the user enters **200**, then when the user enters **9**. (3)
ms: For 200: Gift / Points / Thanks — separate ifs, and 200 clears BOTH bars, then the unconditional Thanks. For 9: just Thanks — 9 clears neither. The design lesson: separate ifs are correct here because a big spender genuinely earns both rewards at once; an elif would wrongly limit them to one. Choosing ifs vs elif is about whether the outcomes can coexist.

q: State the output, and explain the role of the variable `found`. (4)
ms: Output: Yes. Trace: 3 no, 8 no, 12 — match! found becomes True and break ends the search early (7 is never checked — that's the efficiency win). Role of found (2 marks): it's a FLAG that records WHY the loop ended, because after the loop you can no longer tell 'found it' from 'ran out of list' without it. This flag + break + report shape is the standard search pattern — learn it whole.

q: State the output. (3)
ms: Output: X only. Path: the outer test x > 5 passes, so we ENTER the nested block; the inner test y > 5 fails, so the inner else fires. The outer else never runs because its if succeeded. Reading nested ifs: follow one path at a time like a maze, and match each else to the if at ITS OWN indentation level.

q: State the output. (3)
code:
total = 0
n = 17
while n > 0:
    total = total + n % 10
    n = n // 10
print(total)
ms: Output: 8. Trace: n % 10 grabs the LAST digit, n // 10 chops it off. Pass 1: digit 7 (total 7), n becomes 1. Pass 2: digit 1 (total 8), n becomes 0 — loop ends. This is the digit-sum pattern: % 10 reads, // 10 shifts. Recognising the pattern by its %10 / //10 signature saves tracing time in the exam.

q: Two versions of a grading program are shown. State each version's output for mark = 75, and state which version is correct if 70+ should be "A". (4)
ms: Version 1 outputs B; Version 2 outputs A (2). Version 2 is correct (1). Why Version 1 fails: 75 passes the FIRST test it meets (>= 50), gets B, and the chain stops — the A branch is unreachable for every mark, ever. The permanent rule: in elif chains, order bands from most demanding downwards (1). This exact bug, in prices or grades, appears on almost every paper.

q: Trace this program and state the output. Then state in one sentence what the program computes for any list. (4)
ms: Output: 2 2. Trace: 5 odd, 2 even (count 1), 9 odd, 4 even (count 2). Then len(nums) - count = 4 - 2 = 2 gives the odds without counting them separately — one counter and a subtraction covers both. Purpose sentence (1): it displays how many list values are even and how many are odd. Recognise the shape: loop + guarded counter = 'count how many satisfy a condition'.

q: Complete this program so it prints "Hot" above 25, "Cold" below 10, and "Mild" otherwise. Fill in blanks **(A)**, **(B)** and **(C)**. (3)
code:
temp = int(input())
if temp (A) 25:
    print("Hot")
(B) temp < 10:
    print("Cold")
(C):
    print("Mild")
ms: (A) > (1); (B) elif (1); (C) else (1). Why elif and not if: the three outcomes are alternatives — exactly one must fire — and elif guarantees that by stopping at the first match. Why else has no condition: it means 'everything not caught above', which here is precisely 10–25.

q: Complete this program so it prints every multiple of 4 from 4 to 40 inclusive. Fill in blanks **(A)**, **(B)** and **(C)**. (3)
code:
for i in range((A), (B), (C)):
    print(i)
ms: (A) 4 (1); (B) 41 (accept 44) (1); (C) 4 (1). The key mark is (B): range stops BEFORE its second value, so including 40 forces the stop past it — 41 works, 44 works, 40 does not. Say it as a rule: to include N, stop must be beyond N.

q: Complete this validation so it re-asks until a whole number from 1 to 6 (a dice roll) is entered. Fill in blanks **(A)**, **(B)** and **(C)**. (3)
ms: (A) < (1); (B) or (1); (C) > (1). Read the finished condition out loud: 'while the roll is below 1 OR above 6, ask again' — the loop continues while the value is OUTSIDE the range, and outside-a-range conditions always use or (breaking either fence is enough to be invalid).

q: Complete this program so it counts how many of the 10 entered temperatures are below freezing. Fill in blanks **(A)**, **(B)** and **(C)**. (3)
ms: (A) 0 (1); (B) < (1); (C) 1 (1). The shape to memorise: counter starts at 0 BEFORE the loop, and grows by 1 only inside the if-guard. Freezing means strictly below zero, so < not <= — read the scenario's wording for the boundary every time.

q: Complete this sentinel loop so it totals donations until 0 is entered, without counting the 0. Fill in blanks **(A)**, **(B)** and **(C)**. (3)
code:
total = 0
d = int(input())
while d (A) 0:
    total = total (B) d
    d = (C)(input())
print(total)
ms: (A) != (1); (B) + (1); (C) int (1). Why the structure protects the total: the first read happens BEFORE the loop, the test rejects the sentinel before it can be added, and the refill sits at the BOTTOM of the body — so the 0 is tested, never totalled. This read-test-refill ordering IS the sentinel pattern.

q: Complete this program so it prints the characters of `word` one per line, but stops completely if it meets a space. Fill in blanks **(A)**, **(B)** and **(C)**. (3)
ms: (A) word (1); (B) break (1); (C) print (1). Why break and not continue: the task says STOP COMPLETELY — break ends the whole loop, while continue would merely skip the space and carry on. Match the verb in the question to the keyword: 'stop' → break, 'skip/ignore' → continue.

q: Complete this program so it prints every number from 1 to 20 EXCEPT multiples of 5, using continue. Fill in blanks **(A)**, **(B)** and **(C)**. (3)
ms: (A) 21 (1); (B) 0 (1); (C) continue (1). How it works: multiples of 5 leave remainder 0, and continue abandons just that pass, so the print below is skipped for 5, 10, 15, 20 but reached by everything else. Also note (A): including 20 needs the stop at 21.

q: Complete this login: max 3 attempts at the password "open123"; print "In" on success, "Locked" after 3 failures. Fill in blanks **(A)**, **(B)**, **(C)** and **(D)**. (4)
code:
tries = 0
ok = False
while tries < 3 and ok == (A):
    pw = input()
    tries = tries + 1
    if pw == (B):
        ok = (C)
if ok:
    print("In")
(D):
    print("Locked")
ms: (A) False (1); (B) "open123" (1); (C) True (1); (D) else (1). Read the while condition as a sentence: 'keep going while attempts remain AND we're not in yet' — either running out of tries or succeeding makes one side False, and and needs both, so either event exits. The flag ok then tells the code after the loop WHICH exit happened — flags carry the story out of the loop.

q: Complete the nested loops so they print a 4-row, 6-column grid of #. Fill in blanks **(A)**, **(B)** and **(C)**. (3)
ms: (A) 4 (1); (B) 6 (1); (C) line (1). Structure check: rows OUTSIDE, columns INSIDE — the inner loop builds one full row of 6 before the outer prints it and moves on. If you'd swapped 4 and 6 you'd get the transposed grid: always ask 'which loop is the rows?' before filling numbers.

q: Complete this program so it finds whether `target` appears in the list, using a flag, and prints True or False. Fill in blanks **(A)**, **(B)** and **(C)**. (3)
code:
nums = [4, 8, 15, 16]
target = int(input())
found = (A)
for n in nums:
    if n == (B):
        found = (C)
print(found)
ms: (A) False (1); (B) target (1); (C) True (1). The flag logic: assume not-found (False) before looking; flip to True the moment a match appears; the flag can never flip back, so after the loop it truthfully reports whether ANY match occurred. Starting the flag at True instead is a classic planted error — it would report True for everything.

q: Convert this for loop into a while loop with identical output. (3)
code:
for i in range(2, 10, 2):
    print(i)
ms: i = 2 before the loop (1); while i < 10: with print(i) inside (1); i = i + 2 at the end of the body (1). The three-ingredient recipe for any conversion: INITIALISE before, TEST at the top (same boundary the range used — stop stays exclusive, so < 10), UPDATE inside by the step. Forgetting the update line creates the infinite loop — it's the ingredient students drop.
msCode:
i = 2
while i < 10:
    print(i)
    i = i + 2

q: Convert this while loop into a for loop with identical output. (3)
code:
i = 1
while i <= 6:
    print(i * i)
    i = i + 1
ms: for i in range(1, 7): (2 — the <= 6 boundary becomes stop 7, because <= INCLUDES 6 and range EXCLUDES its stop); print(i * i) as the body (1). Conversion rule for boundaries: 'while i <= N' ⇔ 'range(start, N + 1)'. Check your answer by asking: does each version's last printed value match? Both end at 36 — correct.
msCode:
for i in range(1, 7):
    print(i * i)

q: Rewrite these nested ifs as a single if using one condition, keeping the behaviour identical. (3)
ms: if age >= 18 and ticket == "VIP": (2) with print("Lounge access") indented once (1). Why they're equivalent: the inner if only ever runs when the outer passed, so the print needs BOTH conditions — which is exactly what and says in one line. Flattening nests with and is safe ONLY when the inner if has no else; an inner else would need the nest kept.
msCode:
if age >= 18 and ticket == "VIP":
    print("Lounge access")

q: Rewrite this chain of separate ifs as an if/elif/else so that exactly one message prints, and state why the original could misfire. (3)
ms: if speed > 70: Fine / elif speed > 50: Warning / else: OK (2 — order matters: hardest band first). Why the original misfires (1): separate ifs are ALL tested, so speed = 80 passes both > 70 and > 50 and prints Fine AND Warning. elif makes the outcomes mutually exclusive — one driver, one verdict.

q: Write a Python program that reads 12 monthly rainfall values and prints how many months were above 100mm. (4)
ms: Marks: counter initialised to 0 before the loop (1); for loop running exactly 12 times (1); float/int input read inside with the > 100 test guarding the count (1); count printed AFTER the loop (1). This is the pure count-the-hits pattern: pot before, guarded +1 inside, report after. Note > not >= — 'above' excludes exactly 100.

q: Write a Python program that keeps asking for a password until it is at least 8 characters AND contains no spaces, then prints "Set". Use len() and the `in` test (`" " in pw`). (4)
ms: Marks: first input before the loop (1); while condition rejecting bad passwords: len(pw) < 8 or " " in pw (2 — the STAY-in conditions are joined by or because failing EITHER rule means ask again); re-read inside, "Set" printed after (1). Notice the mirror: the acceptance rule is an and ('long enough AND no spaces'); the keep-asking rule is its inverted or.
msCode:
pw = input()
while len(pw) < 8 or " " in pw:
    pw = input()
print("Set")

q: Write a Python program that prints the 8 times table as `1 x 8 = 8` up to `12 x 8 = 96`. (4)
ms: Marks: for loop over 1..12 — range(1, 13) (1, the include-N-stop-N+1 rule); product i * 8 (1); output formatted with all parts: print(i, "x", 8, "=", i * 8) (1); everything inside the loop so 12 lines appear (1). Commas in print insert the spaces for you — the cleanest way to mix text and numbers without type errors.
msCode:
for i in range(1, 13):
    print(i, "x", 8, "=", i * 8)

q: Write a Python program that reads numbers until -1, then prints the biggest and the count of numbers entered (excluding the -1). Assume all real entries are positive. (5)
ms: Marks: biggest and count initialised (0 is safe here because entries are positive) (1); first read BEFORE the loop, while n != -1 (1); count incremented and n > biggest comparison with update inside (2); both results printed after the loop (1). Two patterns snapped together — sentinel loop + running max — which is how nearly all 5-mark designs are built: recognise the bricks, assemble, trace once with e.g. 4, 9, 2, -1 → biggest 9, count 3.
msCode:
biggest = 0
count = 0
n = int(input())
while n != -1:
    count = count + 1
    if n > biggest:
        biggest = n
    n = int(input())
print(biggest)
print(count)

q: Write a Python program that reads a whole number and prints "Buzz" if it divides by 7, "Lucky" if it ends in 7, and "Both" if both are true. Exactly one message must print. (4)
ms: Marks: input read (1); the Both test FIRST — if n % 7 == 0 and n % 10 == 7 (1); elif branches for each single case (1); % 7 for divisibility and % 10 for the last digit both correct (1). The ordering insight: the most SPECIFIC condition must lead the chain, or 77 (divides by 7 AND ends in 7) would be caught by a single-case branch first and "Both" would be unreachable.

q: Write a Python program that prints the numbers 20 down to 2 in steps of 2, then prints "Blast off". (4)
ms: Marks: for with range(20, 0, -2) (2 — start 20; stop 0 so that 2 is included, because the stop is excluded; step -2); print(i) inside (1); "Blast off" unindented after the loop so it appears once at the end (1). Check the endpoints by listing: 20, 18, … 4, 2 ✓ — always verify a stepped range by writing its first and last values.

q: A quiz asks 5 questions; the correct answers are all "B". Write a program that reads 5 answers, counts correct ones, and prints "Winner" for 4 or more, otherwise the score. (5)
ms: Marks: score initialised (1); loop of exactly 5 reading an answer each pass (1); comparison ans == "B" guarding score + 1 (1); AFTER the loop, selection score >= 4 (1); "Winner" or the score printed on the correct branches (1). Note where the if lives: the counting if is INSIDE the loop (per answer); the winner-check if is OUTSIDE (once, on the final score). Placing selections at the right loop-level is what this question is really testing.

q: Write a Python program that reads one word and prints how many times the letter "e" appears in it. (4)
ms: Marks: word read with input() — no int(), it's text (1); counter initialised (1); for c in word: walking the characters with c == "e" guarding the count (1); count printed after the loop (1). The for-each-character loop is the string version of for-each-item — same counting pattern, different collection. Trace with "tree": t no, r no, e yes, e yes → 2.

q: Write a guessing game: the secret is 50. Read guesses until correct; print "Up" for low guesses, "Down" for high; when correct, print the number of attempts. (5)
ms: Marks: attempts counter initialised (1); loop that reads at least once — read before a while guess != 50, or while True with break (1); counter incremented per guess (1); Up/Down selection with the comparisons the right way round — guess < 50 → "Up" (1); attempts printed once correct (1). Sanity-check the hints: a guess of 30 is too LOW so the player must go UP — students reverse these under pressure; test with one example before moving on.
msCode:
attempts = 0
guess = int(input())
attempts = attempts + 1
while guess != 50:
    if guess < 50:
        print("Up")
    else:
        print("Down")
    guess = int(input())
    attempts = attempts + 1
print(attempts)

q: Write a Python program that prints a right-angled triangle of stars with 6 rows (1 star, then 2, up to 6), using nested loops or string repetition. (4)
ms: Marks: outer structure over rows 1..6 — range(1, 7) (1); each row's stars grow with the row number (1); implemented either as "*" * i (string repetition — neat) or an inner loop building the line (1); rows printed one per line (1). Both routes earn full marks; the string-repetition version shows how one Python idiom can replace a whole inner loop. Trace rows 1 and 6 to confirm the shape.
msCode:
for i in range(1, 7):
    print("*" * i)

q: A car park charges £1.50 per hour up to 4 hours, then £1 per extra hour, but never more than £10. Write a program that reads the hours and prints the charge. (5)
ms: Marks: input read (1); selection hours <= 4 → hours * 1.50 (1); else branch: 6 + (hours - 4) * 1 for the longer stays (1); the CAP applied after: if charge > 10: charge = 10 (1); charge printed (1). Order of operations matters — calculate the raw charge first, THEN clamp it; capping inside the branches duplicates logic and invites errors. Trace 3 hrs → 4.50; 8 hrs → 10 (raw 10 exactly); 12 hrs → capped 10 ✓.

q: State the output, then explain why moving `print(total)` one indent to the right would change it. (3)
code:
total = 0
for i in range(3):
    total = total + 5
print(total)
ms: Output as written: 15 — one line, after the loop finishes (1). Indented inside the loop it would print after EVERY pass: 5, 10, 15 — three lines (1). The principle (1): indentation decides ownership; outside the loop = once with the final value, inside = a progress report each pass. This one-indent difference is a recurring 1-mark decider in real papers.

q: State the output when the user enters **-4**. (3)
ms: Output: Negative even. The path: -4 >= 0 is False → the OUTER else block; there, -4 % 2 == 0 is True (yes, negative numbers can be even — -4 = -2 × 2) → "Negative even". Navigating nested if/else: pick the branch at each level like junctions on a route, and never let the surface pattern (four prints) tempt you into evaluating branches you didn't enter.

q: State the output. (3)
code:
n = 6
result = 1
while n > 1:
    result = result * n
    n = n - 2
print(result)
ms: Output: 48. Trace: n = 6 → result 6; n = 4 → result 24; n = 2 → result 48; n = 0 fails the test. It multiplies the EVEN numbers down from 6 (6 × 4 × 2) because the step is -2, not the full factorial — a near-miss designed to catch anyone who pattern-matches 'factorial!' without tracing. Look at the update line before naming the pattern.

q: For each value of n — **10**, **45**, **80** — state the output of this program. (4)
ms: 10 → Low; 45 → Mid; 80 → High (3). The elif chain works like a sieve (1): each value falls through the tests until one catches it — 45 escapes n < 20 but is caught by n < 60; 80 escapes both and lands in else. Notice the bands don't need upper AND lower bounds: 'n < 60' only sees values that already failed 'n < 20', so it MEANS 20–59. That implicit lower bound is the elegance (and the exam point) of chains.

q: State the output. (3)
ms: Output: 5. Why: the nested loops visit all 25 (i, j) pairs, but the guard i == j passes only on the diagonal — (0,0), (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4). Picture the 5×5 grid and shade where the condition holds: turning nested-loop conditions into grid pictures converts hard counting into easy geometry.

q: This program should print the average of the numbers 1 to 10 (which is 5.5), but prints 5.0. Find the fault, name the error type, and correct it. (3)
ms: Fault: range(1, 10) sums only 1..9 (total 45) and then divides by 10 — the stop excluded the 10 (1). Error type: logic (off-by-one) (1). Correction: range(1, 11), giving 55 / 10 = 5.5 (1). Diagnostic tip: when an average or total is slightly low, count the loop's actual passes before touching the arithmetic — nine times out of ten it's the range.
code:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 10):
    total = total + i
print(total / 10)

q: State the output when the inputs are **7**, **7**, **0**. (3)
ms: Output: Streak: 1 / Streak: 2. Trace: first 7 → streak 1 (printed); second 7 → streak 2 (printed); 0 → the while test fails so the body never processes it (no reset, no print — the loop just ends). Sentinels are gatekept at the TOP: whatever the body would have done to 0 never happens.

q: Explain what this program does, line-group by line-group, and state its output for inputs **12** then **18**. (4)
ms: What it does: repeatedly subtracts the smaller from the larger until they're equal — the classical algorithm for the greatest common divisor / highest common factor (1). Trace for 12, 18: b becomes 6 (18-12); then a becomes 6 (12-6); equal → loop ends (2). Output: 6 — and indeed HCF(12, 18) = 6 (1). Exam skill: 'explain what it does' = describe the loop's overall effect, not each keystroke; then verify with the trace.

q: State the output. (3)
ms: Output: False. Why: the flag starts optimistic (True: 'all even so far') and one counter-example — the 3 — flips it forever; nothing ever sets it back. This is the ALL-items-pass pattern: assume True, falsify on any failure. Compare with the ANY-item pattern (start False, flip on success). Which way the flag starts tells you which question the code is answering.

q: State the output when the user enters **3**. (3)
code:
n = int(input())
for i in range(n):
    print(n - i)
print("Go")
ms: Output: 3, 2, 1, Go. Why: i runs 0, 1, 2 and the print shows n − i: 3−0, 3−1, 3−2. A countdown built from a count-UP loop — the subtraction flips the direction. Two ways to build countdowns exist (negative step, or n − i); recognise both so neither surprises you.

q: Write a Python program that reads 6 prices and prints the total, but any price over £100 is capped at £100 before adding. (4)
ms: Marks: total initialised (1); loop of 6 reading a float each pass (1); the cap: if price > 100: price = 100 BEFORE the addition (1); total printed after the loop (1). Order inside the body is the whole question — cap first, add second; adding first then capping the TOTAL is a different (wrong) program. When requirements say 'each item is limited', the fix belongs inside the loop, per item.
msCode:
total = 0
for i in range(6):
    price = float(input())
    if price > 100:
        price = 100
    total = total + price
print(total)

q: Write a Python program that prints all the factors of an entered whole number (the values that divide it exactly). (4)
ms: Marks: n read (1); loop over every candidate 1..n — range(1, n + 1) (1); the divisibility test n % i == 0 (1); factors printed inside the guard (1). Why % is the star: 'divides exactly' ALWAYS translates to 'remainder is zero'. Trace n = 6 → 1, 2, 3, 6 ✓. Loop-over-candidates + %-test is the factor/multiple template for a family of questions.

q: Write a Python program that reads 10 scores and prints the highest, the lowest, and the difference between them (the range). (5)
ms: Marks: FIRST score read and used to initialise BOTH high and low (1 — starting them at 0 breaks on all-high or all-negative data); loop for the remaining 9 (1); two guarded updates — s > high and s < low (2); the three outputs, with range = high − low (1). One initialisation trick serves both extremes: seed from real data, then let comparisons do the work. Trace with 5, 9, 2 (shrunk): high 9, low 2, range 7.
msCode:
s = int(input())
high = s
low = s
for i in range(9):
    s = int(input())
    if s > high:
        high = s
    if s < low:
        low = s
print(high)
print(low)
print(high - low)

q: State the output, and name the two loop-control keywords whose difference this program demonstrates. (3)
ms: Output: 1, 3, 4 (2). i = 2 is skipped by continue (lap abandoned, loop lives on); i = 5 triggers break before printing (loop dead). Keywords: continue and break (1). Seeing both in one loop is the cleanest way to fix the difference: continue removed ONE number, break removed THE REST.

q: Write a Python program that reads a start value and prints the Collatz-style sequence: while the value is not 1, halve it if even (use //), otherwise triple it and add 1 — printing each new value. (4)
ms: Marks: n read (1); while n != 1: (1); the even test n % 2 == 0 choosing n = n // 2 vs n = 3 * n + 1 (1); each new value printed inside the loop (1). Why // and not /: / would drift into floats (3.0, 1.5…) and the == 1 test could misbehave — integer problems deserve integer operators. Trace from 6: 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 ✓.

q: State the output. (3)
ms: Output: 6. Trace one outer pass: j = 1 (total +1), j = 2 (total +1, then break) — the inner loop contributes exactly 2 per outer pass, and j = 3 is never reached. Three outer passes × 2 = 6. Key fact demonstrated: break exits ONLY the inner loop; the outer serenely begins its next pass. If break killed both loops the answer would be 2 — knowing which loop dies is the mark.

q: A student claims these two programs always behave identically. Test both with `n = 0` and state each output, then give the verdict. (3)
code:
# Program 1
n = int(input())
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1

# Program 2
n = int(input())
while True:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
    if n <= 0:
        break
ms: Program 1 with 0: prints NOTHING — the pre-condition test 0 > 0 fails immediately (1). Program 2 with 0: prints 0 once — while True enters unconditionally, prints, THEN discovers it should stop (1). Verdict: not identical; they differ exactly when the loop 'should' run zero times (1). This is the pre-condition vs at-least-once distinction made concrete — and why replacing a while with while-True+break needs care at the boundary.

q: Trace this program for the input list shown and state the output. Then state the everyday name for what it computes. (4)
ms: Output: 91 77.0 (2). First loop: best 70 → 85 → 91 (62 loses). Second loop: total 70 → 155 → 217 → 308; 308 / 4 = 77.0 — note the .0, / always floats (1). Everyday name: the top mark and the average/mean of the scores (1). Reading multi-loop programs: handle each loop as its own mini-program, carry the results forward.

q: Restaurant bill program: read the food total; add 10% service charge only if the total is £30 or more; then add £2.50 per person for cover, reading the number of people; print the final bill to 2 decimal places. (5)
ms: Marks: food total read as float (1); service selection with the boundary INCLUSIVE — total >= 30 → total * 1.1 (1); people read as int (1); cover added: total + people * 2.50 (1); printed with round(bill, 2) (1). Requirement-reading discipline: '£30 or more' = >=, not > — one word in the question sets the operator. Trace £40 + 2 people: 44 + 5 = 49.0 ✓.
msCode:
total = float(input())
if total >= 30:
    total = total * 1.1
people = int(input())
bill = total + people * 2.50
print(round(bill, 2))

q: State the output. (3)
ms: Output: True. What it checks: each character against its mirror — s[0] vs s[4], s[1] vs s[3], s[2] vs itself — and "level" reads the same both ways, so no mismatch ever flips the flag: it's a palindrome test (all-pass flag pattern again). You don't need to pre-know the pattern to score — the flag + mismatch-test structure tells you it's asking 'is the string symmetric?'

q: Write a Python program that simulates a savings goal: read a weekly amount; print the running balance each week until it reaches at least £500; then print how many weeks it took. (4)
ms: Marks: balance and weeks initialised (1); while balance < 500: (1); balance grown by the weekly amount, weeks counted, balance printed each pass (1); weeks printed after the loop (1). The condition faces the GOAL (< 500 keeps saving), and the at-least wording is satisfied because the loop exits the first time the balance ≥ 500 — trace £120/week: 120, 240, 360, 480, 600 → 5 weeks.
msCode:
amount = float(input())
balance = 0
weeks = 0
while balance < 500:
    balance = balance + amount
    weeks = weeks + 1
    print(balance)
print(weeks)

q: State the number of lines this program prints, without listing them all — show the calculation. (3)
ms: 28 lines. Calculation: the inner print runs 6 × 4 = 24 times (2); the separator sits in the OUTER body, so it prints once per outer pass: 6 more (1). 24 + 6 = 28. The skill: attribute each print to its loop level BY ITS INDENTATION, then multiply/add — no listing needed, which is exactly how to handle big nested counts under time pressure.

q: This ticket program has two faults. For each: identify it, name the error type, and give the fix. Requirement: under 5 free; 5 to 15 pays child price £3; 16+ pays £6. (4)
ms: Fault 1: age <= 5 wrongly gives 5-year-olds a FREE ticket — 'under 5' means age < 5 (1); logic/boundary error (1). Fault 2: age < 15 excludes 15-year-olds, who fall to the £6 branch — should be age <= 15 (1); logic/boundary error, fix elif age <= 15: (1). Method: convert each English phrase to an operator FIRST ('under' = <, '5 to 15' = >= 5 and <= 15 — the chain's order supplies the >= half), then check every boundary age: 4, 5, 15, 16.

q: Trace this program and state its output. Inputs, in order: **20, 15, 30, 0**. (4)
code:
cheapest = 0
first = True
price = int(input())
while price != 0:
    if first:
        cheapest = price
        first = False
    elif price < cheapest:
        cheapest = price
    price = int(input())
print(cheapest)
ms: Output: 15. Trace: 20 arrives with first = True → cheapest 20, flag lowered. 15 < 20 → cheapest 15. 30 < 15? No. 0 stops the loop. Why the first flag exists (the real teaching point): a minimum can't safely start at 0 — 0 would 'beat' every real price — so the code uses the FIRST real value as the seed. Same purpose as initialising min to the first item, dressed as a flag; recognise both costumes.

q: Cinema kiosk program. Requirements: show a menu (1 = Standard £9, 2 = VIP £15); validate the choice with a loop until 1 or 2 is entered; read the number of tickets (validate 1–10 the same way); groups of 6 or more get 20% off; print the total to 2 decimal places. (6)
ms: Marks: menu printed and choice validated — while choice != 1 and choice != 2: re-ask (1, and note the AND: it stays wrong only if it differs from BOTH); price selected by if/else from the choice (1); tickets validated with while t < 1 or t > 10: (1, the outside-a-range or); total = price * t (1); group discount with the boundary inclusive — if t >= 6: total * 0.8 (1); print(round(total, 2)) (1). This one question stitches together the whole chapter: two validation loops (and-form and or-form), a selection, and a boundary discount. Trace VIP × 6: 90 → 72.0 ✓.
